terrain.difficultyNotes: Gunstock publishes 44 trails plus 5 glades and the 49 stored here is the two added, which is how the resort presents its 227 acres. The four-tier split is the resort's own. Two percent double-black is honest rather than coy - this is a well-run intermediate mountain with a good top end rather than a hard one, and the 52% blue figure describes it accurately. The important caveat is the glades: all five run on natural snow with no snowmaking, so the 98% coverage figure is coverage of non-glade terrain and the trees open only when the snowpack allows, which in a 120-inch year is not often.

passes.name: No multi-mountain pass
passes.access: Gunstock is owned by Belknap County and operated by the Gunstock Area Commission. It is not on Epic, Ikon or Indy; access is through its own season pass products.

pricing.notes: The ticket figures are 2025-26 rates for adults aged 30-59: $109 weekend and holiday, $94 midweek. The page does not differentiate window from online purchase - it says only to buy online and skip the line - so advanceTypical is null rather than guessed. Night session pricing is not published separately. The season pass figure is the 2026-27 adult (30-59) Winter Prime pass at $879 through 31 October 2026, rising to $1,079 from 1 November; the midweek pass is $529 rising to $629, and the NH college pass $419.

editorial.overview: Gunstock is owned by Belknap County, which makes it one of the only genuinely publicly-owned ski areas in the country, and the arrangement shows in a good way - this is a mountain run for the people who live around it rather than for a pass conglomerate. It sits above Lake Winnipesaukee in Gilford with 1,340 feet of vertical on 227 acres, and the view down the lake from the top is the best base-area view in southern New Hampshire. What Gunstock does better than anything else in this guide for its size is night skiing: 22 trails lit with LED fixtures, Tuesday through Saturday from 3pm, which is roughly half the mountain and includes the Blundersmoke terrain park. Very few places in New England light that much terrain. The daytime skiing is a solid intermediate mountain with a respectable top end off the Tiger chair, five natural-snow glades that open when the snowpack allows, and 98% snowmaking on everything else. What it is not is big or steep, and 120 inches of natural snow means the glades are a bonus rather than a plan. For a Boston-area skier it is under two hours, which is the other half of the appeal.
editorial.snowQuality: One hundred and twenty inches is a modest natural total and Gunstock does not pretend otherwise - it covers 98% of its non-glade terrain with snowmaking and grooms most trails nightly, which is what keeps a mountain at this latitude and elevation reliable. What you ski here most of the time is well-maintained machine snow, and it is genuinely well maintained. The gap is the glades: all five are natural cover only, with no snowmaking at all, and in a typical Lakes Region winter the ropes come down on them for a limited number of days. Gunstock is a mountain to ski for its consistency and its night operation rather than for its snow.
editorial.crowds: Generally light, with a specific and predictable exception. Lift lines are usually confined to the high-speed quad even on busy days - the other seven lifts absorb people well - but Saturdays bring heavy traffic from the Boston-area day-trip catchment, and the quad is where it lands. The night sessions are the interesting case: Tuesday through Saturday evenings draw a local crowd that is smaller and more skilled than the weekend daytime one, and skiing here at 5pm on a Wednesday is one of the quieter good experiences in New Hampshire.
editorial.difficulty: An intermediate mountain with more of a top end than its 2% double-black suggests. Fifty-two percent of the terrain is blue and that is the honest centre of gravity, but the Tiger chair accesses the steepest terrain on the hill and its runs are sometimes left ungroomed specifically to build bump lines, which gives a strong skier somewhere to work. Recoil is the trail regulars name for variety and sustained pitch. The five glades start from the summit with more on the east side and are the genuinely interesting terrain - steep enough to matter, and quiet - but they are natural cover only and closed more than they are open. Nothing here will frighten an expert, and that is not what Gunstock is selling.

keyTrails.name: Recoil
keyTrails.note: The trail regulars name for sustained pitch and variety - the closest Gunstock comes to a run that keeps demanding something of you the whole way down.

keyTrails.name: Tiger
keyTrails.note: The chair that accesses the steepest terrain here, and the zone left ungroomed often enough to build real bump lines. Also lit for night skiing, which is unusual for a mountain's hardest terrain.

keyTrails.name: Blundersmoke
keyTrails.note: The main terrain park, and by the resort's own claim one of the largest night-accessible parks in New England. Small, medium and a few large features.

keyTrails.name: Flintlock to Stonebar
keyTrails.note: The longest run at a mile and a half, and the best way to take in the Lake Winnipesaukee view that is Gunstock's other asset.

keyTrails.name: The summit glades
keyTrails.note: Three glades drop from the summit with more on the east side. All natural snow, no snowmaking, and worth watching the report for.

tidbits: Gunstock is owned by Belknap County - one of very few publicly-owned ski areas in the United States.
Twenty-two trails are lit for night skiing, Tuesday through Saturday from 3pm, using LED fixtures.
Snowmaking covers 98% of the non-glade terrain; the five glades have none.
The base area looks out over Lake Winnipesaukee.
Two lit trails run through the terrain parks, so the freestyle terrain stays open after dark.
It is under two hours from Boston, which is why the high-speed quad queues on Saturdays.
bestFor: A Boston day trip under two hours

moguls.policy: Gunstock grooms most trails nightly, which is the default state of a mountain running 98% snowmaking. The exception is deliberate: sections of the Tiger area are sometimes left ungroomed specifically to build bump lines, so the mountain's steepest terrain is also where its moguls are. There is no permanently ungroomed trail.

namedRuns.name: Tiger
namedRuns.note: Sections of the Tiger terrain are left ungroomed to build bumps, and this is the steepest ground on the mountain. Whether they are there on a given day depends on what the grooming crew decided overnight.

moguls.quality: Modest but genuine, and better than a mountain with a nightly-grooming habit usually manages - leaving the steepest zone alone on purpose produces a proper bump line rather than the leftovers you get where grooming simply ran out of time. The limitation is reliability: because it is a decision rather than a policy, the bumps come and go, and there is no trail here you can count on the way you can count on Wildcat's blacks. The compensating pleasure is that Tiger is lit at night, so this is one of very few places in New England where you can ski bumps after dark.
moguls.bestTiming: Late in a stretch without fresh snow, when the crew has had a few days to let the Tiger terrain build up. Spring, when the surface softens, is the reliable window.
moguls.bumpCulture: No competitive scene. Gunstock's identity is night skiing and its long-running Mountain Meisters race league, and what bump skiing happens here is individual rather than organised.

parks.name: Blundersmoke Park
parks.note: The main park, carrying small, medium and a few large features including the mountain's largest jumps. The resort calls it one of the largest night-accessible parks in New England, and the ski-cross courses it occasionally sets up go here.

parks.name: Side Arm
parks.note: The progression park - extra small and small features, small boxes and simple snow features, aimed at riders taking their first laps through a park.

parks.progression: Two parks and a clean step between them: Side Arm for extra-small and small features, Blundersmoke for everything above. It is a short ladder compared with Loon's five parks or Waterville's six, but for a 227-acre mountain the coverage is sensible and there is no gap where a rider has to jump two sizes.
parks.overview: Twenty-two acres of freestyle terrain spread across green, blue and black trails with features from extra small to large, organised into two named parks. The thing that distinguishes it is the lighting - two lit trails run through the parks, so the freestyle terrain stays open through the Tuesday-to-Saturday night sessions.
parks.reputation: Well regarded regionally and genuinely distinctive on one axis: a night-accessible park of this size is rare in New England, and for a rider who works during the day that matters more than a bigger park two hours further north. Blundersmoke carries the largest features; nobody would rank it against Carinthia or Loon Mountain Park, and it does not need to be ranked against them to be the right choice on a Wednesday evening.
